text: An API, application programming interface, is a web address that returns data instead of a web page. Companies and governments publish APIs for weather, currency rates, public records, and their own systems. If a dataset is available through an API, you can pull it straight into Python, always fresh, with no manual downloads. This lesson covers the core workflow with the requests library, and the habits that keep you out of trouble.

Requests is a third-party library — pip install requests if you don't have it already. We'll use JSONPlaceholder, a free public practice API that needs no account or key and returns made-up fictional data, so it's completely safe to experiment with. Send a get request to its users endpoint, with a 10-second timeout so your code never waits forever. Status underscore code comes back 200 for success; dot-json parses the body straight into a list of Python dictionaries.

That response is a list of nested dictionaries — the address field, for example, contains its own geo dictionary inside it — exactly what json underscore normalize from Lesson 27 is built to flatten. Normalize the data, and you get dotted column names like address dot city sitting right alongside the flat ones. Pull out id, name, and address dot city, and you get a clean, flat little table — from here, everything from the pandas chapters applies directly.

Pass filters as a dictionary through the params argument, rather than gluing them onto the URL string yourself. Request the posts endpoint with params equal to user id 1, and requests builds the full URL for you, with the query string attached correctly and safely encoded.

Many APIs return a limited number of records per request, so you fetch pages in a loop and combine them afterward. JSONPlaceholder supports underscore page and underscore limit parameters, though other APIs use completely different names, so always read the provider's own documentation. Loop over pages 1, 2, and 3, calling raise underscore for underscore status on each response before appending it, then concat all the pieces together with ignore underscore index equals True. Raise underscore for underscore status raises a loud error on any 4xx or 5xx response — far better than silently building a DataFrame out of an error message.

A few habits keep you a good API citizen. Check the status code and set a timeout on every single call, no exceptions. Respect rate limits — many APIs cap requests per minute and answer with a 429 too-many-requests when you go over, so pause between calls and follow the documented limits. Read the terms of use, since data can carry licensing, attribution, or commercial-use rules you need to honor. And cache responses by saving the JSON to disk, so re-running your notebook doesn't repeat requests you've already made.

Some APIs require a key or token to authenticate. Never paste it into a notebook or commit it to a repository — read it from an environment variable instead, and send it in a request header. Pull the token from os dot environ, build an Authorization header with Bearer and the token, and pass that header along with your get request. The exact header name and format vary by provider, so always follow their specific documentation.

To recap: requests dot get with a URL, params, and a timeout fetches data, and dot-json parses it. Pd dot json underscore normalize turns nested JSON into a flat DataFrame. Loop over pages, call raise underscore for underscore status, and concat the pieces together. Respect rate limits and terms of use, cache your results, and always keep keys out of your code. Next: web scraping basics, for when there's no API at all.
